question: Does Georgia maintain a separate, standalone property management license distinct from the standard real estate broker license?
choice_a: Yes -- Georgia requires a distinct Property Manager license issued separately from the Broker license
choice_b: No -- O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1 defines 'Broker' to include performing property management services for a fee, so PM activity requires a broker license (or a licensee acting under a broker), with no separate PM license
choice_c: Yes -- but only in counties with population over 500,000
choice_d: No -- property management in Georgia requires no license of any kind
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1's definition of 'Broker' expressly includes performing property management services for a fee, and 'Property Management Services' is separately defined in the same section; there is no standalone Georgia property-management license -- PM activity must be performed under a broker license.

question: Under O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-30 through 44-7-37, does Georgia statute cap the dollar amount a landlord may charge as a residential security deposit?
choice_a: Yes -- deposits are capped at one month's rent
choice_b: Yes -- deposits are capped at two months' rent
choice_c: No -- Georgia's security deposit statutes impose no statutory dollar-amount cap on deposit size, unlike some states that cap deposits at a multiple of monthly rent
choice_d: Yes -- deposits are capped at $500 regardless of rent amount
explanation: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-30 to 44-7-37 contain no statutory dollar-amount cap on the size of a residential security deposit in Georgia -- a landlord may set the deposit amount by agreement, unlike jurisdictions that statutorily cap deposits at a set number of months' rent.
source_note: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-30 to 44-7-37 (confirmed absence of a dollar cap)

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31, where must a Georgia landlord deposit a tenant's security deposit?
choice_a: Into the landlord's general operating account, commingled with rent receipts
choice_b: Into any account of the landlord's choosing, with no notice obligation to the tenant
choice_c: Into a state-run security deposit trust fund administered by the Department of Community Affairs
choice_d: Into an escrow account established only for that purpose at a regulated bank or lending institution, with the tenant notified in writing of the account's location
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31 requires the security deposit to be placed in an escrow account established only for that purpose at a regulated bank or lending institution, and the tenant must be notified in writing of that account's location.

question: A managing broker deposits all tenant security deposits directly into the brokerage's general operating account rather than a dedicated escrow account, and never notifies tenants of any account location. Which Georgia statute does this violate?
choice_a: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31, which requires a dedicated escrow account at a regulated bank plus written tenant notice of its location
choice_b: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34, which governs only the timing of the deposit's return
choice_c: No statute is violated as long as the full deposit amount is eventually returned
choice_d: O.C.G.A. § 48-6-1, the real estate transfer tax statute
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-31 specifically requires the security deposit to be held in a dedicated escrow account at a regulated bank or lending institution, with written notice to the tenant of that account's location -- depositing funds into a general operating account with no tenant notice violates this section.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34, within how many days of obtaining possession must a Georgia landlord either return the security deposit in full or provide a written itemized statement of deductions?
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34 requires the landlord to return the security deposit, or provide a written statement itemizing the damages and deductions, within 30 days of obtaining possession of the premises.

question: A tenant moves out and the landlord regains possession on June 1. Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34, by what date must the landlord return the deposit or send an itemized statement of deductions, assuming June has 30 days?
choice_d: There is no deadline as long as the landlord eventually responds
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34 sets a 30-day deadline running from the date the landlord obtains possession; possession regained June 1 plus 30 days brings the deadline to July 1.
source_note: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34; timeline computed from the statutory 30-day period

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(c), what is a Georgia landlord's liability for wrongfully withholding a tenant's security deposit, absent a bona-fide non-intentional error?
choice_a: Liable only for the exact amount wrongfully withheld, with no additional penalty
choice_b: Liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld, with no attorney's fees available
choice_c: Liable for a flat statutory fine of $1,000, regardless of the deposit amount
choice_d: Liable for three times (treble) the amount wrongfully withheld, plus reasonable attorney's fees
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(c) makes a landlord liable for three times (treble) the amount of the deposit wrongfully withheld, plus reasonable attorney's fees, unless the landlord's failure resulted from a bona-fide non-intentional error, in which case liability is limited to the actual amount wrongfully withheld.

question: A Georgia landlord wrongfully withholds $900 of a tenant's security deposit in bad faith, with no bona-fide error involved. Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(c), what is the landlord's exposure for the withheld amount alone, before attorney's fees?
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(c) imposes treble-damages liability for a wrongfully withheld deposit absent a bona-fide non-intentional error: $900 x 3 = $2,700, plus reasonable attorney's fees on top of that figure.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(b), what happens if a Georgia landlord fails to provide the required itemized statement of deposit deductions within the statutory time period?
choice_a: The landlord may still withhold the deposit but must pay a small late fee to the tenant
choice_b: The landlord forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the deposit or to sue the tenant for damages
choice_c: The tenant's claim is barred entirely for failing to object in time
choice_d: The itemized statement requirement is automatically waived after 30 days
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(b) provides that a landlord's failure to timely provide the itemized statement of deductions forfeits the landlord's right to withhold any part of the deposit or to sue the tenant for damages to the premises.

question: A Georgia landlord discovers significant damage to a rental unit after move-out but never sends the tenant any itemized deduction statement within the statutory window. Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(b), can the landlord still sue the tenant for the cost of the damage?
choice_a: Yes -- the landlord may always sue for actual damages regardless of the itemized statement requirement
choice_b: Yes, but only if the damage exceeds the deposit amount
choice_c: No -- failing to timely provide the itemized statement forfeits the landlord's right to withhold the deposit or sue for damages
choice_d: No, but only if the tenant paid the deposit in cash
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-35(b) expressly forfeits the landlord's right to withhold any deposit or to sue for damages when the landlord fails to timely provide the required itemized statement -- the landlord in this scenario has lost both remedies.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50, what must a Georgia landlord (or the landlord's agent) do before beginning formal dispossessory (eviction) proceedings against a holdover tenant?
choice_a: Change the locks immediately without any court involvement
choice_b: Shut off utilities to compel the tenant to leave voluntarily
choice_c: Wait a minimum of 90 days from the lease's expiration before taking any action
choice_d: First demand possession from the tenant; if the tenant refuses or fails to comply, the landlord may then file a sworn affidavit before a judge or magistrate to begin dispossessory proceedings
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50 requires the landlord or agent to first demand possession of the premises; only if the tenant refuses or fails to deliver possession may the landlord go before a superior/state court judge or magistrate and file a sworn affidavit to begin the dispossessory process.

question: A property manager wants to remove a nonpaying tenant from a Georgia rental unit by changing the locks while the tenant is at work, without going through any court process. Is this a lawful approach under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50?
choice_a: No -- Georgia's dispossessory process requires first demanding possession, then filing a sworn affidavit before a judge or magistrate if the tenant does not comply; self-help removal is not the statutory path
choice_b: Yes -- self-help lockouts are expressly authorized once rent is 30 days late
choice_c: Yes -- as long as the property manager gives 24 hours' written notice first
choice_d: Yes -- but only for commercial tenancies, not residential
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50 sets out the required dispossessory mechanism -- demand for possession, followed by a sworn affidavit filed before a judge or magistrate if the tenant does not comply -- rather than permitting a landlord or agent to unilaterally lock out a tenant without using that process.

question: In a property management context, which of the following best describes the purpose of a gross lease as opposed to a net lease?
choice_a: In a gross lease, the tenant pays all operating expenses directly, while the landlord pays only rent
choice_b: In a gross lease, the tenant pays a fixed rent and the landlord pays the property's operating expenses (taxes, insurance, maintenance); in a net lease, the tenant pays some or all of those expenses in addition to rent
choice_c: A gross lease and a net lease are simply two names for the identical arrangement
choice_d: A gross lease applies only to residential property, and a net lease applies only to raw land
explanation: Under a gross lease, the landlord is responsible for property operating expenses such as taxes, insurance, and maintenance out of the fixed rent collected, whereas under a net lease structure the tenant assumes responsibility for some or all of those expenses on top of base rent.

question: When screening prospective tenants for a managed rental property, which practice would expose a broker to fair housing liability under generally applicable federal fair housing principles?
choice_a: Applying the same objective income-to-rent ratio and credit criteria uniformly to every applicant
choice_b: Verifying employment and rental history for every applicant using the same process
choice_c: Applying different screening criteria (such as income requirements or background check standards) to applicants based on their race, national origin, or familial status
choice_d: Running a uniform criminal background check policy applied consistently to all applicants
explanation: Fair housing compliance in property management requires that screening criteria be applied uniformly and be based on legitimate, non-discriminatory business factors; applying different standards to applicants because of a protected characteristic such as race, national origin, or familial status is unlawful discriminatory screening.

question: In preparing a market rent analysis for a managed property, which of the following is the most appropriate method for a broker to use?
choice_a: Setting rent solely based on the owner's desired monthly income target, without reference to the local rental market
choice_b: Using the property's original purchase price as the sole basis for setting rent
choice_c: Copying the highest rent advertised anywhere in the metro area, regardless of comparability
choice_d: Comparing the subject property's rent to recently leased comparable properties in the same market, adjusted for differences in size, condition, amenities, and location
explanation: A sound market rent analysis relies on comparable rental data -- recently leased properties similar in size, condition, amenities, and location -- adjusted for differences, rather than owner income targets, purchase price, or the single highest unrelated listing in the market.
source_note: hedge: standard national property-management market-analysis content

question: Which of the following provisions is a core element that should typically appear in a written property management agreement between a broker and an owner-client?
choice_a: The scope of the manager's authority, the manager's compensation structure, the term of the agreement, and the manager's responsibilities for maintenance, reporting, and handling of trust funds
choice_b: A guarantee that the property will never experience a vacancy during the management term
choice_c: A waiver releasing the manager from any obligation to account for rents collected
choice_d: A clause allowing the manager to co-mingle owner funds with the manager's personal funds for convenience
explanation: A well-drafted property management agreement defines the scope of the manager's authority, compensation, term, and the manager's specific responsibilities for maintenance, owner reporting, and proper handling of trust funds -- consistent with the broker-only supervisory and trust-fund-handling responsibilities emphasized in property management practice generally.
source_note: hedge: standard national property-management-contract content, consistent with broker-level PM trust-fund/risk-management responsibilities

question: As part of a broker's risk-management responsibilities in overseeing a property management portfolio, which practice best reduces the broker's exposure to liability for mishandled tenant and owner funds?
choice_a: Allowing individual property managers to keep their own informal, unreviewed records with no centralized oversight
choice_b: Maintaining accurate, regularly reconciled records that clearly distinguish each owner's and tenant's funds, with systematic oversight of trust account activity
choice_c: Depositing all client and tenant funds into a single unsegregated account with the brokerage's operating funds
choice_d: Avoiding written management agreements so that responsibilities remain informal and flexible
explanation: Sound broker-level risk management in property management requires maintaining accurate, well-reconciled records that clearly segregate owner and tenant funds, with systematic supervisory oversight of trust accounting activity -- the opposite of informal, unreviewed, or commingled recordkeeping.
source_note: hedge: standard national broker-level property-management risk-management/trust-account content
